speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: asked the Minister for Communications and Information given the gravity of data protection breaches in the public sector, whether the Personal Data Protection Act should be amended to remove the exemptions for public agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With the gathering pace of digitalisation, we recognised the need to strengthen data protection in the private sector.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: PDPA establishes a baseline standard for data protection in the private sector, balanced against its need to use personal data for reasonable purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: On its part, the Government has always taken seriously its responsibility to protect the data entrusted to the public sector and we continue to strengthen our data governance policies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Since 2001, the Government Instruction Manuals (IMs) already include measures to govern the use, retention, sharing and security of personal data among public agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The data protection standards in PSGA are also aligned with the PDPA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In addition, data collected by the public sector is also protected by specific legislation, such as the Official Secrets Act, the Income Tax Act, the Infectious Diseases Act and the Statistics Act.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: PSGA allows personal data to be managed as a common resource within the public sector for better policymaking and also for more responsive public services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, when a Singaporean applies for financial assistance at a Social Service Office, the frontline officers are able to quickly evaluate his or her eligibility for financial assistance because they have access to data from other relevant agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In this way, we minimise the documents that need to be submitted by the applicant and improve the delivery of public services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In contrast, each private sector organisation is expected to be individually accountable for the personal data in its possession, and there is no expectation of a similar integrated delivery of services across different commercial organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will regularly review the PDPA, PSGA and other legislation to ensure that they remain relevant and effective in safeguarding personal data in both the public and private sectors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have four supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first question is, I acknowledge that the various statutes and the IMs, as the Minister mentioned, do set out standards for the Public Service to comply with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister agree, however, that these instruments, legislation or IMs are usually silent or weak on the recourse that citizens may have if there is a data breach?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They may be strong on penalties for errant officers but, generally, we get silences on the rights of citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The third question is, we talked recently about the SingHealth incident.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The PDPC's judgement in the cyberattack case mentioned that members of the public complained to it that their data had not been adequately protected by SingHealth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: PDPC actually made some findings which will likely lead to improvements on the part of SingHealth and the Integrated Healthcare Information Systems (IHiS) as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps the last question for now is that one of the things that the PDPA does provide is a complaints procedure which I would like the Minister to confirm that this is something that is very useful to the citizens, which does not force the citizens to commence a lawsuit against a Government agency should one suffer damage and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, these are very real advantages of the PDPA which I believe citizens can benefit from.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am not sure all of them were questions because some of them were observations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the key conclusion we have to draw is this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, and that was the thrust of my reply that, one, the public sector and the PSGA, in particular, takes reference, and it is in broad alignment with PDPA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But having said that, there is a clear recognition that the mode of operation and the expectation of how data is used in order to provide an effective and efficient Public Service, implies that we do need a different methodology in the way we govern public sector data governance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why we have this differentiated approach.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In addition to the PSGA, as I had said, we do have other legislations in place.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Just for Members' information, we are by no means alone in this approach.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Canadians, for example, at the federal level, also have different laws in terms of its application to the private sector and its application to the public sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is not about differing standards or somehow having a different threshold when it comes to the public sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, many of the questions that the Member has raised pertain more to whether there are elements of the PDPA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, there is a complaints procedure where they can complain to the PDPC on, for example, the right to data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the Member made the point that the PDPA strikes the balance between the right to data of the individual versus the right to use the data of the enterprises.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Indeed, that is the balance we are trying to strike, whether it is in the public domain or in the private domain.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because essentially, you can say the same sets of considerations apply in the public sector – that we want to ensure individual data is protected, accorded due safeguards, but, at the same time, it should be a common resource that public sector agencies can tap on in order to better serve citizens.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Many of the services that we take quite for granted today actually rely on that backend sharing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, when it comes to a complaints procedure today, there is nothing stopping an individual who feels aggrieved that their data has somehow been mishandled to launch a complaint.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And they have different channels for doing so.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is the process through which we derived a whole set of very detailed recommendations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What the PDPC did, because it received the complaint early in the process, was to say that it will take reference from the COI's process in determining whether there was a breach by the relevant agencies, in this case SingHealth and IHiS, and, if so, what penalty should be meted out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the substantial portion of the recommendations was actually made through the COI process which was, in fact, initiated by the Government, not mandated by any legislation but something that was because of the judgement that was exercised.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The point on recourse comes back to the same thing again.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If a member of the public feels that, in some way, their data has been mishandled, then they have every opportunity to lodge a complaint with the Minister, the Ministry, the relevant department, and action will be taken.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we have to do that, because if we do not, then a lot of our other efforts, in terms of wanting to build a Smart Nation and delivering, harnessing the digital technologies and all these in order to deliver better public services will all be thwarted.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that is exactly why we take this very seriously.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: By and large, the PSGA, in other words, the legislation that governs the public sector data governance, takes reference from the PDPA and we also have other legislation for specific sectoral matters which can also be implied in addition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, the Minister, in his answer earlier, mentioned that for members of the public who are aggrieved that their information has been mishandled by a public agency can always make a complaint.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And the Minister mentioned that it could be to the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Does the Minister not agree that the PDPC itself, which is focused on personal data protection, should have a role to receive such complaints because they are, after all, the domain expert on personal data protection?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second supplementary question is: Minister mentioned the issue of public sector agencies being interconnected and, therefore, there needs to be a different approach.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But I think the SingHealth incident also illustrates some artificiality in what is actually happening in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: If we look at the setup of SingHealth, for example, no doubt, it is not under the definition of public agency under the PDPA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But the fact is that it is very connected to the Ministry of Health (MOH).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In fact, it is owned by MOH Holdings, and there is a frequent, I believe, exchange of data between such healthcare bodies and the parent Ministry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, it would come to a stage, does Minister not agree that, if my data is given to a clinic, for example, under a cluster, I may be able to complain to the PDPC, but once that data goes to the Ministry and the breach happens there, I do not have recourse under the PDPC?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, there is some artificiality in the distinction as far as the healthcare sector is concerned.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The key point I want to emphasise in my response to the Member is this: the term "recourse" for the public has been used several times in the course of this exchange.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The fact of the matter is that you need recourse.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It does not matter whether the recourse is under the PDPC or PDPA, the legislation or there are other established improved mechanisms.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the key point is you must have recourse.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is my point when I said that individuals, depending on where or what circumstances they find themselves in, they can make complaints.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the case of the Government, the Government Technology Agency (GovTech), for example, is overall in-charge of the security and safeguard systems for data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And GovTech is the agency that does many of the reviews and ensures that the Government agencies are in compliance with the IMs and other provisions and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Moreover, there is also the Auditor-General's review as well, which occurs from time to time, and it includes security.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: My point is that members of the public should not at all be concerned that they do not have recourse.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They do, and, in fact, they have a multiplicity of recourse.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I would add that, in the case of the public sector, they probably have more channels and more avenues of recourse in some ways, compared to what you see in the context of the private sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because essentially, for private sectors, you go to the PDPC, or you take out a specific legal action against the company on your own.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Here, you have got more options because you can go through the PDPC.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It would be referred to the relevant agencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: You can go to GovTech, you can go to the Ministry that oversees the relevant department, you can also make a Police report if you feel that it warrants such action.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And, if anything, we impose a higher set of standards.
